meta.title: Home Depot, *Aisle* by Aisle
meta.description: An illustrated, interactive walk through Acquired's Home Depot episode: 19 aisles, watercolor plates, live charts, and 20 business lessons that print on a receipt.
meta.dek: Two fired executives, a banker who smelled an opportunity, and a merchant who reportedly drove a forklift through a wall built the best-performing American stock of the last 45 years. An illustrated walk through Acquired’s Home Depot episode, and the business lessons stacked on every shelf.
meta.byline: A companion to the episode by Ben Gilbert & David Rosenthal · released September 14, 2026

intro: The episode has 19 chapters, so this page has 19 aisles. The bar at the top tracks where you are in the episode’s 3 hours and 35 minutes. Each aisle ends with a shelf tag holding one lesson; as you read, the tags drop into your cart, and they print on a receipt at checkout.

sections.label: Intro
sections.headline: The best stock nobody brags about

blocks.text: Ben and David open with a claim that sounds like trivia until you check it. From its IPO in September 1981 to today, Home Depot has been the single highest-returning equity in the American stock market. Put $1,000 in at the offering, reinvest the dividends, and you have about $17 million. The same $1,000 in the S&P 500 became about $170,000. Home Depot went public a year after Apple, and on that same $1,000 bet it beats Apple too.

The hosts say this was among the most requested episodes in the show’s history, with emails arriving every week for two or three years. Their question for the next three and a half hours: Home Depot is the only specialty retailer in the world that sits in the same universe as Costco, Walmart and Amazon. Why did this one company, selling lumber and lightbulbs, work so uniquely well?

blocks.title: What 45 years of compounding looks like
blocks.subtitle: Drag through the years. Both paths are drawn at the constant rate that connects the episode’s endpoints.
blocks.note: Shaded bands mark each CEO’s tenure. Switch to the log scale and steady compounding becomes a straight line.
blocks.label: Home Depot

blocks.title: Compounding is boring in any one year.
blocks.body: At about 24% a year, money doubles roughly every three years and two months. Fourteen doublings separate $1,000 from $17 million. No single year of it looks like much; the result comes from never stopping.

sections.label: Bernie Marcus’s early career & meeting Arthur Blank
sections.headline: A pharmacist from Newark

blocks.text: Bernie Marcus grew up poor in 1930s Newark, the son of Jewish immigrants from Russia, and was the first in his family to go to college. He wanted to be a doctor. Money pushed him to pharmacy instead, and pharmacy pushed him into retail, where he discovered he liked the store more than the counter. He rose through the New York discount chain Two Guys, and in 1972 the Los Angeles conglomerate Daylin made him CEO of its hardware subsidiary, a chain called Handy Dan.

At Daylin he met Arthur Blank, a sharp numbers man with a background, like Bernie’s, in the drugstore business. Bernie made him his finance chief at Handy Dan. It was the start of a partnership that would run for almost three decades: Bernie the showman and salesman, Arthur the operator who knew where every dollar went.

The idea came from a visit down the coast. Bernie went to see a retail friend in San Diego, a man named Sol Price, whose Price Club warehouse sold everything from tires to tuna in giant quantities at prices nobody could match. A Handy Dan store carried about 8,000 items. Price’s model suggested a hardware warehouse could carry 25,000, bought directly from manufacturers, at rock-bottom prices. As the episode puts it, the eventual business plan was “really pretty much exactly, just clone Price Club.”

note.definition: Stock-keeping unit: one distinct item a store carries. A 3-inch and a 4-inch brass hinge are two SKUs.

blocks.title: The best ideas are often borrowed from the next aisle over.
blocks.body: Sam Walton said he stole more ideas from Sol Price than from anyone. So did Costco’s founders. Bernie’s move was to see that the warehouse model, proven on groceries and tires, had barely touched hardware, where selection and price mattered even more.

sections.label: Ken Langone & Handy Dan
sections.headline: The banker who bought a stock at two times earnings

blocks.caption: Before he founded EDS in 1962, Perot sold computers for IBM.

blocks.text: Ken Langone came from nothing, an Italian-American kid from Long Island who talked his way onto Wall Street. While he was still young he won the job of sole manager for the IPO of Ross Perot’s Electronic Data Systems in 1968, the deal that made his name, and his relationship with Perot.

Years later a CEO he trusted pointed him at Handy Dan: a well-run hardware chain trapped inside a parent company that was in trouble. Langone looked it up. The stock was trading around $3 while the company earned about $1.50 a share, a price of two times earnings. He flew to Los Angeles the next day and kept buying until he owned nearly 20% of the company. That is how he met the man running it, Bernie Marcus.

note.definition: Share price divided by profit per share. At 2×, a buyer pays two years of profit for the stock; the market usually pays 15 to 20.

blocks.caption: The world before the warehouse: the tool aisle of a Hechinger lumber and hardware store in Washington, D.C. Hechinger was one of the regional chains Home Depot would outgrow and outlast.

blocks.title: Back the operators, not the parent.
blocks.body: Handy Dan was cheap because its owner was struggling, not because the stores were. Langone bought the people a CEO had vouched for, at a price set by somebody else’s problems, and the people turned out to be the asset.

sections.label: Ken buys Handy Dan, Bernie & Arthur fired
sections.headline: Kicked by a golden horseshoe

blocks.text: In early 1978, Langone did something he rarely did: he sold. The buyer was Sanford Sigoloff, the turnaround specialist running Daylin, a man whose reputation for slashing earned him the nickname “Ming the Merciless.” Sigoloff and Bernie did not get along. A few months later he fired Bernie, Arthur and their audit manager, officially over a fund an employee had set up to fight a union drive at stores in San Jose. Bernie always called the charge trumped up.

Bernie was 48 and, by his own account, devastated. Langone saw it differently, and his line has become part of Home Depot legend: Bernie, he said, you have just been kicked in the ass with a golden horseshoe. Now go build the warehouse store you keep talking about.

blocks.caption: “You have just been kicked in the ass with a golden horseshoe.” Ken Langone to Bernie Marcus, 1978, as both have long told it.

blocks.title: A setback can remove the reason not to try.
blocks.body: The warehouse idea already existed. What it lacked was founders with nothing to lose. Langone answered the firing with a plan and an offer to raise the money, which turned a bad week into the most valuable startup in retail.

sections.label: Ross Perot almost buys Home Depot
sections.headline: The $223 billion Cadillac

blocks.text: Langone took the idea to the richest man he knew. Ross Perot agreed to put up $2 million for 70% of the new company. Then he started asking about the details, and one detail stuck: Bernie was driving an old company Cadillac. Perot’s executives drove Chevrolets. In Bernie’s telling, Perot put it simply: “My people don’t drive Cadillacs.”

It was not really about the car. Bernie realized that with 70% of the company, Perot would be the boss of every decision, down to the parking lot. They walked away. Asked about it years later, Perot paused and said only, “Everybody has their own stories.” The hosts ran the back-of-envelope math on what that 70% would be worth now: about $223 billion.

items.caption: The offending vehicle, more or less: a 1970s Cadillac Coupe DeVille.

blocks.title: Who would have owned Home Depot
blocks.subtitle: Same $2 million either way. Toggle between Perot’s offer and the money Langone raised instead.
blocks.note: Accounts of Langone’s syndicate differ. The $223 billion figure is the hosts’ playful estimate, not a valuation.

scenarios.label: Perot’s offer
scenarios.text: $2 million for 70%. Perot would have controlled the board and, as the Cadillac suggested, the details. By the hosts’ estimate, that stake would be worth about $223 billion today.

scenarios.label: What happened
scenarios.text: The same $2 million from about 40 investors, in one account of the terms. Management kept nearly half and its independence.

blocks.title: Control is part of the price.
blocks.body: Perot’s money came with Perot. Seventy percent for $2 million was cheap capital and expensive control. The Cadillac was a preview of every argument to come, and Bernie read it correctly.

sections.label: Pat Farrah & the HomeCo interlude
sections.headline: The fourth founder was going broke

blocks.text: With Perot gone, Bernie and Arthur went looking for proof that a home-improvement warehouse could work. They found it in Los Angeles, in a store called HomeCo, run by what the episode calls a wild man named Pat Farrah. HomeCo was everything they had imagined: huge, cheap, crammed with product, buzzing with customers. It was also insolvent, because Pat was not paying his suppliers.

The merchandising was genius and the finances were a mess. Bernie and Arthur could fix the second part. When HomeCo went under, they brought Pat in as the merchant, the fourth founder. His partners compared him, without irony, to Michelangelo. One story has him needing to remove a wall, failing to get a permit, and driving a forklift through it, then calling it an accident.

items.name: Bernie Marcus
items.description: CEO, salesman, the voice of the company and its culture until 1997.

items.name: Arthur Blank
items.description: Finance and operations. Knew the numbers in every store. CEO from 1997.

items.name: Ken Langone
items.description: Raised the seed money, ran the board’s Wall Street side, recruited later CEOs.

items.name: Pat Farrah
items.description: The merchant. Made a store feel full, cheap and alive.

blocks.title: Hire for the thing someone does best, and cover the rest.
blocks.body: Pat Farrah had just run his own store into insolvency. Bernie and Arthur hired him anyway, for the one skill nobody did better, and let Arthur supply the discipline Pat lacked. Vision, money, merchandise and controls: four jobs, four people.

sections.label: First stores & early model
sections.headline: Empty paint cans, ten feet high

blocks.text: First, a name. A marketing consultant pitched “Bad Bernie’s Build-All,” which went nowhere. The wife of one of Langone’s investors suggested “The Home Depot.” The consultant was not a total loss, the hosts note: he is the one who suggested the company adopt orange. It would stand out, and they could buy cheap canvas meant for circus tents and use it for signage.

blocks.caption: Orange started as a cost decision: canvas meant for circus tents made cheap, loud signage.

blocks.text: On June 22, 1979, the first two Home Depots opened in Atlanta, in former Treasure Island discount stores that J.C. Penney sublet to them. The company had about $2 million, not nearly enough to fill a warehouse. So Pat filled it with illusion. Empty boxes went on the high shelves. Empty paint cans were stacked ten feet high to suggest bottomless inventory.

The opening newspaper ad never ran as planned, so staff stood in the parking lots handing out $1 bills to lure people inside. Another legend has Pat on his knees at 4 a.m. polishing the floors before opening. The stores lost about $1 million in 1979 and made about $1 million in 1980.

items.label: Bills handed out to get people in the door
Height of the empty paint-can stacks

blocks.title: Look abundant before you are.
blocks.body: A warehouse store sells the feeling of endless selection and rock-bottom price. On day one Home Depot had neither in full, so it staged both. The stacked cans were a promise the company then spent decades keeping.

sections.label: Home Depot goes public & expands
sections.headline: From two stores to a billion dollars

blocks.text: Home Depot went public on September 22, 1981, at $12 a share, a market value of roughly $32 million. Then it started opening stores across the South. Sales passed $1 billion in 1986. By 1989 Home Depot had passed Lowe’s to become the largest home-improvement retailer in the country.

The one real stumble came early. In 1984 the company bought nine Bowater Home Centers in Texas, Louisiana and Alabama for about $40 million. The stores, the staff and the habits did not fit. Earnings fell 42%, debt rose to about $200 million, and the stock dropped.

blocks.title: Net sales, the founders’ era
blocks.subtitle: Fiscal years 1979–1997, billions of dollars.
blocks.note: Rounded from Home Depot annual reports.

blocks.title: Buying stores is not buying a culture.
blocks.body: Bowater added nine stores in one stroke and produced Home Depot’s first big earnings drop. The things that made a Home Depot a Home Depot, the people and the way they treated customers, were not included in the purchase price.

sections.label: Home Depot’s unique operating system
sections.headline: The format was easy to copy. The people were not.

blocks.text: The longest stretch of the episode is about how the stores actually worked, because that is where the hosts locate the advantage. The warehouse format was the visible innovation, and every competitor copied it within a few years. The operating system underneath it, as an analysis the episode cites argues, was the lasting edge.
Part one: margin you choose not to take

A traditional hardware store bought through distributors and marked goods up to something like a 45% gross margin. Home Depot bought direct and ran at about 30%, then gave the difference back to customers as lower prices. Bernie insisted on one price for everyone: “We were priced right for everyone, not just a select group.”

note.definition: The share of each sale left after paying for the goods. Selling a $55 item for $100 is a 45% gross margin.

blocks.title: The same item at two kinds of store
blocks.subtitle: The store pays $55 for an item. The traditional store keeps a 45% gross margin. Set the warehouse margin.
blocks.note: Margins are the episode’s rough figures for the era; the $55 cost is illustrative.

outputs.label: Volume to match the old store’s profit

blocks.text: That last number is the catch. At a 30% margin a warehouse needs nearly twice the unit volume to earn the same gross profit dollars as a traditional store. The low price is what brings the volume. And the volume is what makes the low price affordable, because bigger orders earn better terms from manufacturers and spread the fixed cost of a giant store across more sales. That loop is the flywheel.

blocks.title: The warehouse flywheel
blocks.subtitle: Tap a step. Each one feeds the next.

steps.label: Lower prices
steps.text: Bought direct, priced at about 30% gross margin instead of 45%, with one price for everyone.

steps.label: More shoppers
steps.text: Homeowners and contractors come for price and stay for the advice of ex-tradespeople.

steps.label: More volume
steps.text: Each giant store moves far more goods than a neighborhood hardware store, and every new store makes the company’s orders bigger.

steps.label: Better costs
steps.text: Huge orders earn better terms from manufacturers. Rent, staff and systems are spread over more sales.

steps.label: Reinvest
steps.text: Instead of keeping the savings as profit, pass them back as lower prices, more associates and more selection.

blocks.text: Part two: plumbers in orange aprons

The second half of the system was the people in the aisles. Home Depot recruited former plumbers, electricians and carpenters, who traded the higher but unreliable pay of contracting for steady hours and work that was easier on the body. The company ran how-to clinics in the stores to teach homeowners to do jobs themselves.

The company’s favorite story is about a washer. A customer comes in to buy an expensive new faucet. The associate asks what is wrong with the old one, sells him a part that costs pennies, and shows him how to install it. The customer later comes back for a full kitchen remodel.
Part three: the CEO at the bottom

All of this was organized by a diagram the company still talks about: the inverted pyramid. At the bottom is the CEO, “just this tiny little triangle,” and at the top, “the big thick level is customers.” Everyone in management exists to support the people in orange aprons.

blocks.title: Which way up?
blocks.subtitle: Home Depot’s org chart, and the conventional one it inverted.
blocks.text: Customers at the top, the associates who serve them next, and every layer of management beneath, down to the CEO.
blocks.flipped_text: The conventional chart: the CEO on top, layers of management in the middle, customers at the bottom.

blocks.title: Margin you don’t take is a moat.
blocks.body: Every point of margin Home Depot left on the table became lower prices, which became volume, which became better costs. A competitor who wanted to match the price had to match the volume first.

blocks.title: Sell the washer, not the faucet.
blocks.body: An associate who saves a customer money today earns the remodel later. Trust was the product behind the products, and it depended on hiring tradespeople and not paying them on commission.

sections.label: Arthur Blank takes CEO & early cracks
sections.headline: The startup that was now a $24 billion company

blocks.text: In 1997, almost two decades after the founding, Bernie decided it was time to declare victory and handed the CEO title to Arthur. On paper everything was working. Sales were about $24 billion and the company was opening more than a hundred stores a year.

Underneath, the hosts point to problems that would “come back to bite Home Depot pretty quickly.” The company still ran with the informality of a startup, and Lowe’s had found a gap: brighter, tidier stores that made a point of courting women, who were making more and more of the decisions about home projects.

blocks.title: What works at 100 stores can crack at 1,000.
blocks.body: Informality was an asset when Bernie could walk every store. At a thousand stores it became inconsistency, and a competitor noticed which customers felt unwelcome and built stores for them.

sections.label: The Bob Nardelli era
sections.headline: A turbine man in a hardware store

blocks.text: In late 2000, Bob Nardelli lost the race to succeed Jack Welch at General Electric to Jeff Immelt. Ken Langone sat on GE’s board, and within days Nardelli was CEO of Home Depot. The episode calls him “the GE guy through and through,” and he ran the company like one.

items.caption: Where Nardelli learned to manage: GE Power Systems.

blocks.text: Nardelli brought Six Sigma, dashboards and centralization. He folded nine regional buying offices into one, centralized purchasing and replenishment, and replaced many experienced tradespeople with lower-paid part-timers; associates per store fell from about 200 to about 170. Revenue doubled. The stock went nowhere while Lowe’s more than doubled.

note.definition: GE’s statistical method for cutting defects in manufacturing, aiming for fewer than 3.4 per million.

blocks.title: What doubled, and what didn’t
blocks.subtitle: Fiscal 2000 to fiscal 2006, indexed to 100.
blocks.note: Revenue includes HD Supply. Associates per store and the Lowe’s gain are as cited in summaries of the episode.

blocks.title: Efficiency can eat the product.
blocks.body: Every metric Nardelli tracked improved, while the thing customers came for, a knowledgeable person in an orange apron, got scarcer. The stock noticed before the dashboards did.

blocks.text: At the May 2006 annual meeting in Wilmington, Delaware, the board stayed away. Nardelli ran the meeting himself in about half an hour, with large timers limiting shareholder questions to a minute each. The meeting turned simmering frustration about his pay into a national story. On January 3, 2007, Nardelli was out; his exit package was widely reported at about $210 million.

blocks.title: Legitimacy is an asset you can’t see on the balance sheet.
blocks.body: Six years of a flat stock did not end Nardelli’s tenure. A half-hour meeting that treated the owners as an inconvenience did.

sections.label: Frank Blake’s turnaround: crisis & culture
sections.headline: The quiet lawyer who stopped building stores

blocks.text: The board replaced Nardelli with Frank Blake, a lawyer who had worked at GE and served as deputy secretary of Energy. He took over in January 2007, just as the housing market began to collapse. He put money back into the people on the floor, and every Sunday he wrote dozens of handwritten thank-you notes to store associates who had solved a customer’s problem.

blocks.caption: Home Depot calls its Atlanta headquarters the Store Support Center, a name that follows from the inverted pyramid.

blocks.text: Then he stopped growing. Blake sold HD Supply in 2007 for about $8.5 billion, effectively froze the store count, and redirected the cash into existing stores, the supply chain and buybacks. The company repurchased roughly 30% of its stock, mostly at $30 to $50 a share.

note.definition: A company buys its own shares and retires them, so each remaining share owns a bigger slice of future profits.

blocks.title: Stores open at fiscal year-end
blocks.subtitle: The Nardelli years added a store every two days. The Blake years added almost none.

blocks.title: In a crisis, invest in the front line.
blocks.body: Blake inherited a housing crash and a demoralized staff, and chose to spend on associates, not cut them. The notes cost nothing; the message they carried was the whole strategy.

blocks.title: Stop growing to start compounding.
blocks.body: More stores had stopped meaning more value. Blake made the existing stores more productive and bought back about 30% of the company at low prices.

blocks.text: Early Home Depot had no distribution centers at all. Vendors shipped straight to the stores. Under Blake, the company built rapid deployment centers that flow goods out to stores, and Craig Menear pushed further with an $11 billion plan to connect stores, warehouses and the website. When the pandemic arrived, sales went from about $110 billion in fiscal 2019 to about $151 billion in fiscal 2021. The hosts’ verdict: Home Depot today “would be toast without them.”

note.definition: A flow-through warehouse: goods arrive by the truckload and leave for stores, sorted, within a day or two.

items.caption: A rapid deployment center in Lake Park, Georgia.

blocks.title: Net sales, all 47 years
blocks.subtitle: Highlighted: the pandemic surge the supply chain had to absorb.

blocks.title: Build the boring network before you need it.
blocks.body: Distribution centers looked like pure cost when Home Depot started building them. A decade later they were why a $110 billion retailer could absorb a $40 billion surge in demand.

sections.label: Home Depot today: Pro & DIY
sections.headline: The customer who shops every day

blocks.text: Home Depot today has about 2,350 stores and did $164.7 billion in sales in its most recent fiscal year. Roughly half now come from professionals: contractors, remodelers, roofers and property managers.

blocks.caption: Approximate share of sales by customer type, as described in the episode.
Engineered lumber on the orange racking: the aisles pros come for.

blocks.text: Under CEO Ted Decker, Home Depot made the largest acquisition in its history to chase that customer: SRS Distribution, for $18.25 billion in 2024. In 2025 SRS bought GMS for about $5.5 billion. Along the way, Home Depot outlasted nearly everyone it ever competed with.

blocks.title: The competitors’ graveyard
blocks.subtitle: Warehouse home-improvement chains that once fought Home Depot for the same customers.

items.title: Builders Square
items.caption: Kmart’s warehouse chain, closed by 1999. This former store now wears a Home Depot sign.

items.title: Also gone
items.caption: regional and national rivals that closed or liquidated

blocks.title: Follow the customer who buys every week.
blocks.body: Frequency beats ticket size. The pro already supplied about half of Home Depot’s sales from inside its stores; SRS and GMS buy the delivery networks that serve the rest of the pro’s job.

blocks.text: The things that made a company special when it was small often hold it back at scale. Some companies, like Costco, Rolex and Hermès, “fight gravity.” But sometimes the right move is to abandon the old habit. Which of Home Depot’s founding quirks were the product, and which were scaffolding?

blocks.title: Kept or changed?
blocks.subtitle: Seven things that made early Home Depot special.

items.text: Vendors ship straight to every store; no distribution centers
items.explanation: Changed, and rightly. The hosts: Home Depot today “would be toast without them.”

items.text: Former tradespeople in orange aprons giving real advice
items.explanation: Kept, after a near miss. Nardelli cut them; Blake reinvested.

items.text: Opening new stores as the main engine of growth
items.explanation: Changed. Blake effectively froze the store count.

items.text: The inverted pyramid: customers and associates above the CEO
Nine regional buying offices with local autonomy
items.explanation: Changed. Centralized buying underpins the scale economies the hosts rank first.

items.text: One price for everyone, no special deals for contractors
items.explanation: Mostly changed, as pros became about half of sales.

items.text: Founder-era informality, including after-hours partying in the stores
items.explanation: Changed. Charming at 50 stores, untenable at 2,000.

blocks.title: Know which quirks are the core.
blocks.body: Specialness comes as a bundle. Part of it is the product; part is scaffolding you needed to get here. Nardelli cut the product, the people, and kept the scaffolding. Blake did the reverse.

blocks.text: Ben calls scale economies “the biggest one.” Switching costs matter for pros, and store-brand tool batteries add a little lock-in. Branding counts mostly with pros and serious do-it-yourselfers. The twist: the profitability gap with Lowe’s has seen “a very dramatic convergence over time.”

blocks.title: Home Depot’s powers, as the episode weighs them
blocks.subtitle: Filled bars show how much weight the hosts give each power.
blocks.note: Dashed tiles are powers we found no argument for in the episode materials we could verify.

items.name: Scale economies
items.definition: Per-unit costs fall as volume grows.

items.name: Switching costs
items.definition: Leaving costs the customer more than staying.
items.verdict: Real for pros; tool batteries add lock-in.

items.name: Branding
items.verdict: Mostly with pros and serious DIYers.

items.name: Counter-positioning
items.definition: A model incumbents can’t copy without hurting themselves.

items.name: Process power
items.definition: Embedded ways of working that take years to replicate.

items.name: Network economies
items.definition: Each customer makes the product better for others.

blocks.title: Scale is a power, not a guarantee.
blocks.body: Being nearly twice Lowe’s size buys Home Depot better costs. It has not stopped Lowe’s margins from converging.

sections.label: Quintessence: why it got so big
sections.headline: America’s houses keep getting older

blocks.text: The hosts call their answer a several-part equation, and the first part is the American house. From 1940 to 1980 the median age of the US housing stock held steady at about 23 years. Then it climbed: 25 by 1990, 30 by 2000, around 40 today. David points out that China’s housing market is larger than America’s but a terrible market for home improvement.

items.caption: A street of 1960s Levitt houses in Bowie, Maryland.

blocks.title: Median age of US homes
blocks.subtitle: Years.
blocks.note: 1940–2000 as cited in the episode; today from the 2022 American Community Survey via NAHB.

blocks.title: Why it got so big

terms.label: Old American houses
terms.text: A giant, owner-occupied, wood-framed housing stock that gets older every year.

terms.label: Warehouse prices
terms.text: Sol Price’s model applied to hardware: buy direct, 25,000 items, a 30% margin.

terms.label: People who know
terms.text: Ex-tradespeople, no commissions, and the inverted pyramid.

terms.label: Scale
terms.text: Nearly twice Lowe’s revenue and the best supplier terms.

terms.label: The Pro
terms.text: About half of sales, a customer who buys every week.

terms.label: Capital discipline
terms.text: Blake’s pause on store growth and buybacks at $30 to $50.

blocks.title: Pick a market that grows while you sleep.
blocks.body: Every house in America gets a year older every year. Home Depot’s demand rides on the age of the housing stock, not just on new construction.

closing.headline: Your receipt
closing.text: The episode closes, as Acquired always does, with carve-outs. For those, and for the full three and a half hours, listen to the episode. Here is everything you picked up on the way through; tap any line to go back to its aisle.

about: An independent, illustrated companion to Acquired’s Home Depot episode, not a transcript. It follows the episode’s 19 chapters and timestamps. Quotations come from published transcript excerpts; the narration around them is drawn from the chapter list, published summaries and public records. Lesson framings are our own synthesis.
